title: The lowest deck elevation for a Maine city's April to May 2027 wharf-rebuild work trestle that high water is expected to reach on no more than one tide
subdomain: climate and weather extremes (coastal extreme water levels: the expected number of high waters reaching each candidate deck elevation over a known April to May 2027 window)
prompt_shape: one dial (the deck elevation on a nine-step pile schedule) with the expected tides at the chosen elevation and the one below; five survival tides with dates and levels; six years of street closures with those at the street's flooding level; a bar chart over the schedule

distractors.why_relevant: wind and pressure drive the storm surge on top of the tide
distractors.why_unused: the surge the forecast needs is measured at the gauge itself; no figure reads the airport record
distractors.ruled_out_by: the design basis sets every level at the gauge

distractors.why_relevant: the river's April snowmelt peak falls in the work window
distractors.why_unused: the gauge's readings already carry whatever the river adds at Cutler Wharf; no figure reads it
distractors.ruled_out_by: the design basis sets every level at the gauge

distractors.why_relevant: the harbormaster's own hourly readings of the water on the same pier
distractors.why_unused: the design basis and both asks take the gauge's readings; the board is hourly on its own zero
distractors.ruled_out_by: the design basis section 2 (the gauge's highest 15-minute reading)

sources.origin: constructed for this task by task178/generator/build.py (seeded, deterministic) around a fictional Maine coastal city (Port Tessaly), its tide gauge, harbormaster's office and public works department. No real organisation's records or person is depicted. The tide predictions follow the real astronomy; the storms on the record are placed on the dates of real Gulf of Maine storms but their levels are constructed.
